title: FLEX and Sentinel-3C launched
bodyText:
FLEX and Sentinel-3C launched — ESA / Applications / Observing the Earth, 15/09/2026.

Flight VV30 lifted off on 15 September at 03:21 (14 September at 22:21 local time).

A launch adapter called Vespa allowed both satellites to be stacked inside the Vega-C fairing for launch. Positioned on top of Vespa, Sentinel-3C was injected into orbit first, followed by FLEX approximately one hour later.

Following the satellites’ separate deployments, ESA’s European Space Operations Centre in Germany received the all-important first signal from each satellite, confirming that both had been safely released from the rocket and had established contact with ground control.

Mission controllers will now spend the coming days conducting the ‘launch and early orbit phase’, meticulously checking and verifying the health and performance of both satellites and confirming that all systems are functioning as expected.

ESA’s Director of Earth Observation Programmes, Simonetta Cheli, said, “Today’s launch is the culmination of years of scientific innovation, engineering excellence and international cooperation.

“Developed within ESA’s FutureEO programme, FLEX is a research mission that will advance our understanding of plant health and the role of photosynthesis in the carbon and water cycles. Sentinel-3C is the third satellite in the Sentinel-3 series, systematically measuring Earth’s oceans, land, ice and atmosphere to support Europe’s Copernicus Services.

“Preparing and launching two satellites together is no easy task. My thanks go to the many experts who have contributed throughout both satellites’ development, testing and preparation for launch, and who have worked tirelessly to ensure that both satellites have reached orbit safely.”

FLEX to reveal the hidden activity of Earth’s vegetation

FLEX, the latest Earth Explorer mission, is ESA’s first satellite designed specifically to measure photosynthetic activity from space. Its Fluorescence Imaging Spectrometer will detect the extremely faint fluorescence emitted by plants as they absorb sunlight during photosynthesis.

title: 24小时欧洲航天动态：织女星-C双星发射升空，多项目稳步推进
bodyText:
北京时间2026年9月15日9时21分，欧洲在法属圭亚那库鲁航天中心的ELV发射台，由意大利Avio公司研制的织女星-C（Vega C）小型运载火箭执行VV30发射任务，采用瞬时发射窗口点火升空，整个发射与载荷部署过程持续近2小时，最终按计划将欧洲空间局（ESA）的Sentinel-3C与FLEX两颗卫星送入预定的太阳同步轨道，任务取得圆满成功。

本次任务的轨道参数为倾角98.6度、轨道高度约810公里，这一轨道设计能够让两颗卫星对全球地表实现全覆盖观测，且可以保证卫星每日在同一地方时经过同一观测地点，为长期连续的地球环境监测提供稳定的轨道条件。根据任务流程，火箭起飞后55分28秒，AVUM+上面级完成第二次点火，在起飞后1小时00分49秒，重1143千克的主载荷Sentinel-3C率先完成分离；在起飞后1小时56分03秒，重397千克的FLEX卫星完成分离。载荷部署全部完成后，火箭上面级进行第五次点火，执行末级离轨处置操作，主动再入大气层焚毁，全程符合欧洲空间碎片减缓规范，避免产生长期滞留轨道的太空垃圾。

Sentinel-3C是ESA哥白尼计划（Copernicus Programme）Sentinel-3卫星家族的第三颗卫星，由泰雷兹阿莱尼亚航天公司（Thales Alenia Space）研制。作为欧洲全球环境与安全监测体系的核心组成部分，Sentinel-3系列卫星承担着海洋、陆地、大气多要素综合观测的职能。此前该系列的Sentinel-3A、Sentinel-3B卫星分别于2016年、2018年从俄罗斯普列谢茨克航天发射场，采用基于SS-19洲际导弹改装的Rockot运载火箭发射升空，目前已在轨运行超过8年和6年，逐步进入寿命后期。

Sentinel-3C与后续待发射的Sentinel-3D将承担起任务接续的职责，把Sentinel-3系列的连续观测数据记录延伸至2030年代，为全球气候变化研究、海洋生态监测、灾害应急响应、农业估产等领域提供长期稳定的数据源。该卫星搭载的标准化仪器套件，包括海洋和陆地表面温度辐射计、海洋颜色成像仪、合成孔径雷达高度计、微波辐射计等，可实现对海平面高度、海表温度、海洋水色、陆地植被覆盖、湖泊水位、极地冰盖变化等参数的高精度观测，是目前全球地球观测体系中不可或缺的组成部分。

本次任务搭载的FLEX（Fluorescence Explorer，荧光探测卫星）同样由泰雷兹阿莱尼亚航天公司建造，是ESA“地球探索者”计划的第八颗科学卫星，其核心载荷为Floris荧光成像光谱仪。该仪器能够捕捉到植物光合作用过程中释放的肉眼不可见的太阳诱导叶绿素荧光信号，这一信号直接反映了植物的实际光合效率与健康状态，突破了传统遥感仅能观测植被覆盖度、叶面积指数等表观参数的局限。

FLEX卫星入轨后，将与Sentinel-3系列卫星形成编队观测，结合Sentinel-3提供的温度、植被指数等同步数据，科学家可以精准反演全球不同生态系统的植被胁迫状况，比如干旱、高温、病虫害对农作物和森林的影响，量化陆地生态系统的碳汇能力，进一步明确植物光合作用在全球碳循环、水循环中的作用，为气候变化模型优化、农业生产管理、生态保护政策制定提供关键的科学数据支撑。

title: NOAA’s flood mapping tool now covers nearly 100% of U.S.
originalTitle: NOAA’s flood mapping tool now covers nearly 100% of U.S.
bodyText:
Experimental Flood Inundation Mapping provides valuable guidance for decision-makers and public

NOAA's flood inundation map (left) depicting the forecast for flooding extent in New London, Wisconsin, and a photo of flooded streets in New London (right), dated April 17, 2026. (Image credit: NOAA NWS)

NOAA’s National Weather Service announced today that Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM), a revolutionary tool for predicting river flooding, is now available on an experimental basis to nearly 100% of the U.S. population. This is a massive expansion from FIM’s prior coverage of 60% of the country.

FIM produces estimates of land area covered in water based on model forecast river flows and current conditions that predict where flooding impacts may occur in the following days. It’s a tool for forecasters, emergency managers and the public that alerts users to the latest river and stream flooding conditions.

“Inundation maps are a critical tool for assessing the impacts of flooding,” said NOAA Administrator Neil Jacobs, Ph.D. “NOAA prioritized expanding FIM to ensure that nearly every American can access detailed information beyond the expected river crest height. These maps further support NOAA's mission to protect lives, safeguard property, and strengthen our national economy.”

FIM puts river and stream flooding on the map at a neighborhood scale. It depicts flooding potential along 3.3 million river miles throughout the continental U.S., U.S. territories and Hawaii. For the most recent expansion, FIM’s new coverage areas include: the southeastern U.S. coast and Florida; Great Lakes region; New England; the Rocky Mountains; the Dakotas; and western Nebraska.

title: Galileo achieves first-ever civil authenticated GNSS position using Signal Authentication Service (SAS)
bodyText:
European GNSS Service Centre (GSC) news, 17 September 2026.

On 16 September, Galileo achieved a major milestone in satellite navigation resilience by demonstrating the first-ever civil GNSS position authenticated through both navigation data and ranging information. The demonstration used the Galileo Signal Authentication Service (SAS) concept, with five Galileo satellites transmitting encrypted signal components over Europe. Receivers on the ground successfully processed these signals to compute an authenticated position fix, demonstrating a new level of protection for civil satellite navigation.

On 16 September, between 14:00 and 16:00 UTC, five Galileo satellites—E06, E21, E23, E34 and E36—encrypted one of their signal components, the E6-C signal at 1278.75 MHz, normally transmitted in the clear. Several Galileo SAS receivers deployed at different locations successfully processed these signals in combination with Galileo Open Service Navigation Message Authentication (OSNMA) . For the first time, a civil GNSS receiver was able to process authenticated navigation data and ranging measurements from at least four satellites simultaneously and compute an authenticated position fix.

A significant part of the demonstration took place during Jammertest on the island of Andøya, Norway, where controlled GNSS jamming and spoofing tests are conducted using real over-the-air signals. This provided a unique opportunity to evaluate Galileo SAS under both nominal conditions and many types of spoofing.

During the spoofing tests, conventional receivers were deceived and reported false positions, while the Galileo SAS receiver detected the attack and maintained a trusted position solution based on authenticated Galileo signals.

Historically, civil GNSS receivers have had limited means to verify that the signals they use genuinely originate from navigation satellites. Galileo addressed part of this vulnerability through OSNMA, declared operational in 2025, which authenticates the navigation data transmitted by Galileo satellites. SAS complements OSNMA by protecting the other fundamental source of information used to compute a GNSS position: the ranging measurements.

title: New datasets expand the Climate Data Store’s window on Earth’s changing climate
bodyText:
Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implemented by ECMWF — press article, 17 June 2026.

The Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) has expanded its Climate Data Store ( CDS ) with a new suite of datasets. Spanning the atmosphere, land, ocean, cryosphere and water cycle, these additions provide new opportunities to explore how the Earth system is changing and how those changes affect people, ecosystems and infrastructure. Of the new additions to the CDS, some datasets extend climate records further back in time, others deliver sharper regional detail, while others translate climate observations into practical information relevant to topics such as water resources, heat stress and energy systems, helping users better understand the real-world impacts of climate variability and change. Let's take a closer look.

On land, the Global land surface atmospheric variables from 1718 to present from comprehensive in-situ observations dataset offers one of the longest meteorological records available through the CDS. Drawing on observations from weather stations around the world, it provides harmonised and quality-controlled records of key atmospheric variables spanning more than three centuries. The dataset supports investigations into long-term climate variability and change, while also providing an important observational foundation for the development and validation of climate datasets and reanalyses.

Land-based stations available in the latest version of the Global land surface atmospheric variables from 1718 to present from comprehensive in-situ observations, with sub-daily data. Source: C3S

The historical picture is further strengthened by the ORAS5 global ocean reanalysis monthly data from 1958 to present dataset , which reconstructs ocean conditions by assimilating observations with advanced ocean and sea-ice modelling. Covering more than six decades, ORAS5 provides a consistent record of ocean temperature, salinity, currents, sea level and sea-ice properties, supporting research into ocean variability, heat uptake, circulation patterns and the ocean's role in climate change.

title: August was the joint warmest month ever recorded globally, with temperatures once again exceeding 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels
originalTitle: August was the joint warmest month ever recorded globally, with temperatures once again exceeding 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels
bodyText:
Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) Climate Bulletin, implemented by ECMWF — published 16 September 2026.

August was the joint warmest month ever recorded globally, with temperatures once again exceeding 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels

August 2026 was the joint hottest month on record worldwide, tied with July 2023, as reported in the latest Climate Bulletin by Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) 1 . The month also saw the average sea surface temperature (SST) over the extra-polar ocean – between 60°S and 60°N – reach a record high. This new record can be explained by global heating from burning fossil fuels and rapidly increasing SSTs in the equatorial Pacific, which were associated with strong El Niño conditions.

Global-average surface air temperature (°C) for 2023 (orange), 2024 (yellow), and 2026 (dark red). All other years between 1940 and 2025 are shown with grey lines. Data source: ERA5. Credit: C3S/ECMWF.

Globally, the average surface air temperature in August was 16.96°C, making it the hottest month ever recorded (for all calendar months), tied with July 2023. Notably, this temperature was 1.65°C higher than the estimated 1850-1900 pre-industrial baseline for the month, putting the world once again over 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels. The last time this value was exceeded was less than a year ago, in November 2025. Additionally, it was the warmest August ever recorded, surpassing the previous joint August record, which was set in 2023 and 2024.

The month marked the end of the world's joint hottest June to August period on record, tied with 2024. August also saw the end of western Europe's warmest summer ever recorded, which exceeded the previous long-standing record set in 2003. Western Europe's summer was marked by a succession of intense heatwaves across the region – a sequence that began exceptionally early and continued throughout the season.

title: Uncovering the Valleys Hidden Below Greenland’s Ice
bodyText:
NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day, published 28 September 2026 — 4 min read.

A new map of the terrain beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet links hundreds of valleys that previous maps missed or left fragmented.

Instruments: ICESat-2 — ATLAS Model Topics: Glaciers & Ice Sheets Topography Visualization and Mapping A newly developed method for mapping the bedrock beneath Greenland’s ice sheet reveals the island’s hidden topography. Among the most striking finds are long, straight valleys in the west-central region, some mapped for the first time and others extending farther inland than previously known (inset 3). NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, based on data from Chartrand et al . Greenland is capped with a vast ice sheet that spans 1.7 million square kilometers (656,000 square miles) and measures more than 3 kilometers (1.9 miles) at its thickest point. Below all this ice lies a landscape human eyes have never seen directly. But a newly developed method for mapping this hidden bedrock has produced the most detailed and accurate view of it yet.

The new map reveals an expansive network of valleys carved into the surface beneath the Greenland Ice Sheet. Many of the features formed well before most of the ice above them existed, offering new context for the island’s geologic history—and potentially helping scientists refine projections of the ice sheet’s future. Scientists described the newly mapped valleys in a NASA-led paper published in Geophysical Research Letters .

The map, shown above, was derived from a method called Ice Flow Perturbation Analysis. As ice flows over a valley or ridge, the topography leaves a faint signature on the ice surface. Satellites map the ice surface in fine detail, and scientists can use these subtle bumps and dips to infer the shape of the landscape buried below. The work aims to improve future versions of BedMachine Greenland , a high-resolution dataset of the terrain beneath the ice sheet.

title: Fire Cloud with a Pileus on Top
bodyText:
Scientists captured rare observations of an ephemeral pileus cloud hovering over a smoke-infused cloud that rose above a wildfire in Montana.

Scientists captured rare observations of an ephemeral pileus cloud hovering over a smoke-infused cloud that rose above a wildfire in Montana.

In the false-color image (right) active fires appear pink and yellow, burned areas brown, clouds white, and smoke blue-purple. MASTER images by RoseAnne Dominguez, annotated by Michala Garrison. In summer 2026, scientists took to the air to intercept and study the towering, smoke-infused clouds that wildland fires sometimes create. But during an August 11 flight over the Sand Creek fire in Montana, they came back with a bonus—observations of an ephemeral pileus cloud hovering atop one of the towering fire clouds.

Smooth, veil-like pileus clouds are well-known to atmospheric scientists and cloud lovers and regarded as signs of especially vigorous convection . title: Three Earth Explorer candidates go forward
bodyText:
Today, ESA’s Programme Board for Earth Observation took the decision to pave the way for three mission concepts to move forward to the next stage of development taking into account both their scientific relevance and programmatic considerations.

The decision follows the User Consultation Meeting held in July, where four mission concepts underwent detailed scrutiny by the scientific community. Building on the outcomes of this important consultation, ESA’s Advisory Committee for Earth Observation (ACEO) provided their advice on the scientific merits of each mission, ranking them in the following order: ECO, Keystone, CryoRad, Hydroterra+.

Rene Forsberg, on behalf of the ACEO, said, “ECO would target global mean Earth Energy Imbalance (EEI), the most fundamental climate variable, and widely recognised as the most important longstanding knowledge gap in quantifying ongoing climate change and would assess the effectiveness of climate mitigation measures.”

Acknowledging the scientific and societal relevance of EEI, ESA and its Member States set science first by giving the extremely challenging ECO mission concept the opportunity to be further investigated in the framework of the Earth Explorer 12 activities.

Highlighting the relevance of the Keystone concept, Prof. Forsberg noted, “By providing the first global direct observations of atomic oxygen together with co-located measurements of temperature, wind and relevant atmospheric constituents in the 50–250 km altitude range, Keystone would address fundamental knowledge gaps in this underexplored part of the atmosphere.”

As an additional benefit, Keystone would also detect metal from space debris entering the atmosphere, which is projected to increase exponentially in the future.

title: ESA awards contracts for Europe’s EOGS blueprint
bodyText:
These activities are funded by the European Commission and are integral part of Element 1 of ESA’s European Resilience from Space for Earth Observation (ERS-EO) programme – a new programme decided at the Ministerial Council in November 2025.

The new ERS initiative is a strategic effort by ESA and its Member States to strengthen Europe’s resilience, security and autonomy through space-based capabilities, while jointly and promptly addressing critical capability gaps.

ERS has a system-of-systems vision and brings together complementary capabilities in Earth observation, positioning-navigation-timing and secure connectivity.

The Earth observation pillar of the ERS initiative, ERS-EO, is a dual-use programme and prepares for the European Commission’s future EOGS programme, which is planned to begin in 2028 under the next Multiannual Financial Framework.

It is foreseen that EOGS will provide secure, reliable, timely, persistent and targeted space-based Earth observation data to enhance situational awareness to support preparedness, decision-making and action by the EU and its Member States in the fields of security and defence, while reinforcing existing and planned capabilities.

EOGS will comprise satellites, ground infrastructure, data and information, processing facilities, and distribution infrastructure. EOGS will also draw on commercial services, the sharing of Member States’ own capacities and complementary core capacities developed specifically for and owned by the EU.

title: Earth from Space: Venetian Lagoon
bodyText:
ESA - Earth from Space: Venetian Lagoon Applications Earth from Space: Venetian Lagoon 25/09/2026 2083 views 64 likes 528974 ID Like Download HI-RES JPG [1.61 MB]

This true-colour image of the Venetian Lagoon in northern Italy was acquired by the IRIDE satellites on 17 May 2026. It shows the city of Venice, with its distinctive Grand Canal curving through the historic centre, surrounded by the blue waters of the lagoon and a number of islands.

Venice came to prominence as a maritime republic and seafaring continues to be an important part of the city’s identity, as well as a key form of local transport. The white trails left by boats are clearly visible in some of the busy waterways around the lagoon – including on the south side of the city, near the Murano islands to the north and the Vignole islands to the east.

As well as its famous canal networks, the lagoon’s landscape also includes mud flats, salt marshes and shallow tidal waters. Sediment suspended in the water causes parts of the image to appear bright blue, while the dark blue is where the water is clearer. The sea is a darker shade of blue in the lower-right corner of the image, where Venice Lido, with its white-sand beach, borders the Adriatic Sea.

title: What’s in a name? Naming things in OpenStreetMap
bodyText:
Almost everything has a name and OpenStreetMap volunteers have mapped 115 million names .

In OpenStreetMap, the verbal identifier with which people refer to something is documented by the name= tag. This usually is the most common name in the local language and is the most obvious name of the feature. For example, if you are in France and map a road called “Rue des Beaux-Arts”, you add name=Rue des Beaux-Arts so that everyone knows what that road is called.

There are many map styles based on OpenStreetMap data. On www.openstreetmap.org , we display “osm-carto” style by default, with a layer switcher for many others.

There are a few simple rules that the OpenStreetMap community follows, including:

name= is typically the commonly used name in the local language. A street in Paris has as name= its French name, not the name in English.

name= should be a proper name – not a description or a reference id.
